name: Bimin
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bimin (bimi1240) is not in the catalog. Both sweep items are Glottolog misattachments: Villarejo et al. 2012 (GSR stress sensor, Sensors, doi:10.3390/s120506075) and Yamakoshi et al. 2008 (driver stress detection, IEEE EMBS, doi:10.1109/iembs.2008.4649346) are biomedical-engineering papers on physiological stress, irrelevant, priority none. The real stress statement for Bimin is already on file from the earlier audit pass: Weber & Whitney 1999 Bimin Phonology Essentials, sec. 4 p. 5 (PDF p. 8), which states that stress and high pitch always co-occur and are phonemic, gives four minimal pairs distinguished by stress position, and notes phrasal re-stressing within utterances; reading = lexically contrastive (unpredictable) stress fused with high pitch. Weber 1997 Grammar Essentials adds only that clitics are unstressed (p. 16); Healey 1964 gives family-level 'all Mountain-Ok languages appear to have contrastive lexical pitch' (p. 61) with no Bimin examples. Weber 2003 Bimin OPD (6 pp.) remains unobtainable (SIL 403 on both hosts, no Wayback snapshot), priority medium since it could only refine the 1999 statement. Crossref DOI lookups and SIL/Wayback retries were done by curl. Record appended to

new_statements.quote: Stress and high pitch always go together and are phonemic, as shown in the following examples. 8) a. /boko'líf/ [boko'Ríp] ‘say.2/3PL’ b. /’bókolif/ [‘bókoRif] ‘be.FUT.2/3PL’ 9) a. /’kókmen/ ‘big-head’ b. /kok'mén/ ‘close by’ 10) a. /’síNam/ ‘flying fox’ b. /si'Nám/ ‘far away’. Although a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables this word within an utterance might change the stress to a different syllable or even lose it in favor of a semantically more important word in the context. Within an utterance it is rather a phrase (whether noun or verb phrase) carrying a stress than single words. ... There is a very limited number of words which do have a contrastive tone - or rather high pitch.
new_statements.citation: Weber, Thomas & Henry Whitney. 1999. Bimin Phonology Essentials: Bimin Language (Bim Weng / Nimtew Weng). Ms., SIL PNG, Ukarumpa. (SIL Language & Culture Archives item 43829)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

Section 4 'PITCH/STRESS/ACCENT' is on printed p. 5 = PDF p. 8, continuing to p. 6, exactly as the locator says. The prose of the quote is there verbatim: 'Stress and high pitch always go together and are phonemic, as shown in the following examples.'... 'Although a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables this word within an utterance might change the stress to a different syllable or even lose it in favor of a semantically more important word in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (realised together with high pitch) is phonemic/lexically contrastive: its position is not predictable and distinguishes minimal pairs (initial vs final stress in di- and trisyllables); the transcribed word list shows stress on initial, medial or final syllables item by item. No default position rule is given. The authors add that only a small number of words actually contrast by pitch/stress and the functional load is low.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described; 'minor stress' is mentioned only at utterance level (e.g. a minor stress on the first syllable of a non-focal word in a sentence).
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics have no stress of their own and lean on the preceding word (Grammar Essentials 1997 p. 17); the clitics sako/tako/tewe have a more stressed first syllable. Contrastive high pitch limited to 'a very limited number of words' with low semantic load.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word in isolation (citation form): 'a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables'; in connected speech stress is assigned per phrase, may move to another syllable or be lost depending on information structure/speaker intention. Stress and high pitch are treated as a single prosodic prominence (pitch-accent-like).
new_statements.identity_note: Weber & Whitney 1999 describe Bimin = 'Bim Weng' (main valley, SE Sandaun Province; Bim and Kuskis phratries) with notes on the southern 'Nimtew Weng' dialect (Western Province; Kasan and Kuel phratries); both are the language-level unit bimi1240 (ISO bhl); data mainly from Bim Weng speakers (Akalu village area). Healey 1964's 'Bimin' (Wonggop valley clans Bimin, Kuskusmin, Kwelmin, Kasanmin) is the same language but he gives no Bimin-specific prosodic statement.

Although a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables this word within an utterance might change the stress to a different syllable or even lose it in favor of a semantically more important word in the context. Within an utterance it is rather a phrase (whether noun or verb phrase) carrying a stress than single words.
new_statements.citation: Weber, Thomas & Henry Whitney (1999). Bimin Phonology Essentials: Bimin Language (Bim Weng / Nimtew Weng). Ms., SIL PNG, Ukarumpa, March 1999. iii+11 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives item 43829.
new_statements.reading: Bimin word stress is lexically contrastive (phonemic, not predictable from position): the same segmental string differs in meaning by which syllable is stressed, and stress is realised as high pitch (stress and high pitch are one feature). At the utterance level stress is phrasal and can move or disappear for pragmatic reasons. A handful of words additionally contrast by high pitch alone (fián 'flea' vs fian 'big'). For catalog coding this is 'unpredictable/lexical stress (pitch-accent-like)', not fixed initial/penultimate/final.

sources.note: Sec. 4 'Pitch/stress/accent' (p. 5): stress and high pitch always co-occur and are phonemic; minimal pairs by stress position ('bókolif vs boko'líf, 'kókmen vs kok'mén, 'síNam vs si'Nám, 'áluue vs a'lúue); a word in isolation usually has one audible phonemic stress, but in utterances stress is phrase-level and may shift or disappear; only a very limited number of words carry contrastive high pitch, low functional load. Word list in sec. 3.3 marks stress on varying syllables (initial, medial, final).

sources.quote: Clitics are a closed class. They do not have their own stress, but lean on what precedes them. In Bimin orthography clitics are written as separate words.
sources.note: Ch. 2 phonology sketch (pp. 6-7) covers segments only. Ch. 4 Clitics p. 16: clitics 'do not have their own stress, but lean on what precedes them'; p. 17: sako/tako/tewe 'do have a more stressed first syllable'. No statement of default word-stress position; secondary to Weber & Whitney 1999.
